The chime on the headset was a polite, predictable sound – a tiny, metallic notification of another soul needing a lifeline. I was halfway through fielding a call from a young man named Daniel, paralyzed by the fear of failure after dropping out of college, when the next one came through. It was anonymous.

“Hello?” I said, my voice calibrated to a blend of warmth and professional detachment. “This is Liam at the Haven Center. How can I help you today?”

A pause, longer than usual. Then, a voice – choked, fragmented – “I… I don’t know.”

That was often the starting point. “It’s okay,” I said gently, following protocol. “You don’t have to tell me anything you don’t want to. But I’m here if you need to talk.”

The person, who identified only as “Silas,” began to slowly unravel. A messy, painful tapestry of loneliness, of a feeling of being utterly and irrevocably lost, of a constant, nagging belief that he was a burden to everyone around him. He’d been struggling for months, he said, a dark cloud settling over his life with each passing day. He was having thoughts, vivid and insistent, of just… not being here anymore.

I listened, really listened, mirroring his emotions, validating his pain. I guided him through grounding exercises, reminding him of his breathing, of the tangible things around him – the chair he was sitting in, the air in the room, the sound of the rain outside. It was a delicate dance, balancing empathy with the firm, unwavering line of professional boundaries. I stayed on the line for nearly an hour, patiently coaxing him back from the edge, offering resources, reassuring him that he wasn’t alone. 

Finally, he said, “Thank you. Really. I… I don’t know what I would have done without you.”

The dust was a perpetual grey. It coated everything – my sarcophagus, the meticulously arranged collection of ancient texts within, the perpetually chilly air of my underground chamber. It was, frankly, irritating. And it was a damned good camouflage. The zombie apocalypse hadn’t exactly been a strategic masterstroke for me, Valerius Morbus, Arch-Necromancer, but it had provided a rather… convenient distraction.

Before, I’d been preoccupied with petty squabbles over ancient artifacts, arcane knowledge, and the occasional territorial dispute with rival sorcerers. Now, the world was simply *gone*. Reduced to a shuffling, groaning mass of the recently deceased, all vying for the same decaying resources. A rather crude, predictable, and profoundly boring enemy. 

The problem was, they didn’t *see* me. Not really. Centuries of meticulously cultivated mystique, of manipulating kings and controlling armies, had trained me to be utterly invisible to the casual observer. And a shambling horde was remarkably oblivious to the presence of a being several hundred years old, bound by undeath to a single, exceptionally comfortable sarcophagus. 

“Honestly,” I muttered to Bartholomew, my familiar – a exceedingly grumpy raven who had, inexplicably, survived the initial wave of chaos and chosen to remain in my service. “The sheer lack of intellectual curiosity is astounding.”

Bartholomew merely ruffled his feathers and glared from his perch atop a grimoire detailing the proper ritual for summoning a minor demon. “They’re zombies, Valerius. They don’t *think*.”

“That’s precisely the point, you insolent avian!” I retorted, adjusting the cowl concealing my withered face. “They represent a complete abdication of reason. A societal collapse of the most pathetic sort.”

The rain was, predictably, awful. It was the kind of persistent, depressing drizzle that seemed to seep into your bones and cling to everything like a mournful ghost. I was walking home from my dead-end job at the library – shelving returns, mostly – when I saw it. 

It was small, unassuming. About the size of a hefty notepad, bound in a unremarkable grey leather. It lay nestled amongst a pile of discarded newspapers outside a small, independent bookstore called “Second Chances.” I’d never noticed it before. Curiosity, a depressingly frequent companion, nudged me to pick it up. 

The cover was blank except for a single, subtly embossed symbol: a tiny, stylized shrug. Beneath it, printed in a unassuming, slightly faded black font, were the words “Mild Inconvenience Note.”

I dismissed it initially. It looked… ridiculous. Like a gag gift. But then, something compelled me to open it. The pages were blank, of course, but as I stared at the first page, a small, almost imperceptible mark appeared. A tiny, blue ink smudge, forming the word “Toothpaste.”

I blinked. I rubbed my eyes. I stared harder. The smudge was still there.

I hesitantly wrote, “The microwave will not heat anything.” on the next page. Instantly, a small, dark grey stain bloomed on the digital clock radio across the street, effectively rendering it useless. It was… unsettling. And undeniably, profoundly inconvenient.

My initial reaction was disbelief, swiftly followed by a frantic, illogical need to test it. I’d heard the stories, of course. The Death Note. Ryuk. Light Yagami. It was all fictional, a elaborate, terrifying internet hoax. But this… this was different. This was… smaller. Less dramatic. More… frustrating.

I tried again. “The bus will be twenty minutes late.” Within minutes, a announcement crackled over the station speakers informing passengers of severe delays due to “unforeseen mechanical issues.”

The sterile white of the Pre-Judgment waiting room was profoundly unsettling. It was less a room, more a holding cell designed to erase any lingering hope. Rows of chairs, arranged with chilling precision, faced a enormous, opaque screen that occasionally flickered with images of… well, I wasn’t entirely sure. Twisted landscapes, screaming faces, and things that defied description swam across it, triggering a primal urge to cover my eyes. I’d been here for what felt like an eternity – though the official timer displayed a measly 37 minutes – and the anxiety was a thick, suffocating blanket.

I wasn't here for the scenery. I was here for a spectacularly, unbelievably bad idea.

I had chosen Satan as my attorney.

It had seemed like a perfectly logical, darkly humorous solution. After a lifetime of regret – a career wasted, relationships burned, opportunities missed – I reasoned that if I was going to face eternal damnation, I was going to do it with a professional. A *skilled* professional. And frankly, the idea of a meek, fluttering angel whispering platitudes about repentance was utterly offensive.

The receptionist, a woman with eyes that had clearly seen too much and a face etched with bureaucratic despair, had simply stared at my request with a impassive expression. “Mr. Finch, you understand the… protocols involved?”

“Perfectly,” I’d replied, trying to project an air of confident defiance. “I’m looking for the most effective defense possible.”

The rain in Havenwood was always grey. It clung to everything – the boarded-up storefronts, the rusted swing sets in the park, the perpetually damp faces of the residents. It mirrored the state of everything else, really. Havenwood wasn’t a place you *moved* to; it was a place you ended up. A place where hope went to die, quietly, under a blanket of unrelenting drizzle. 

My name is Silas, and I’m a tracker. Not a good one, not anymore. I used to be one of the Rangers – protectors of the Children. But that was before. Before the Rot.

The Rot started subtly. A little less color in the crayons, a touch more silence from the puppets. Then, the Children began…changing. Their laughter became hollow, their eyes clouded. They stopped playing, stopped speaking, just stared. And they drew. Always drew. Horrible things. Twisted figures, faces consumed by darkness, landscapes of unending grey. 

It was Pinocchio that started it, naturally. The show had been a staple for generations, a comforting lie in a town built on despair. We, the Rangers – a ragtag group of former child psychologists, disillusioned teachers, and a few genuinely good people – were supposed to be the guardians of that lie. We monitored the broadcasts, ensured the show remained wholesome, a beacon of innocence in a rotting world. 

Now, Pinocchio was a legend. A cautionary tale whispered in hushed tones. The original, pristine version was a locked archive, inaccessible. All we had was the Rot. The corrupted, twisted version. 

I used to believe in the magic. I used to believe in the talking puppet who longed for a real nose. Now, I just believed in tracking. Tracking the Children who were gone, absorbed by the Rot, and tracking the source.

The air in the Grand Salon was thick with anticipation, a palpable tension woven with the scent of expensive sandalwood and something subtly metallic – fear, perhaps? Around the enormous, circular table, seated in meticulously arranged chairs upholstered in deep crimson velvet, were the initiates. Men. Powerful men. Politicians, CEOs, military leaders, heads of international organizations – all lured into the Obsidian Circle with promises of knowledge, influence, and ultimately, control. They were the apex of their respective secret societies, the ones who pulled the strings, dictated policy, and shaped the world’s direction. And tonight, they were about to learn the *true* puppeteers.

Across the room, bathed in the cool, unwavering glow of strategically placed chandeliers, sat Seraphina. She was an anomaly within the Circle, a woman of indeterminate age, dressed in a simple, impeccably tailored black suit that somehow commanded attention without drawing it. Her face was serene, almost unsettlingly so, and her eyes, a startling shade of violet, seemed to absorb rather than reflect the light. She was the Grand Matron, the leader of the Obsidian Circle – the organization that had, for centuries, quietly orchestrated the machinations of every other clandestine group on the planet.

“Welcome,” Seraphina’s voice was cool, resonant, and utterly devoid of emotion. “You’ve all passed the tests. Demonstrated ambition, ruthlessness, strategic thinking – the qualities deemed essential for influence. You believed you were at the summit of power, shaping events, mastering the world. You were… misguided.”

A murmur of indignant protest rippled around the table. Senator Davies, a man renowned for his aggressive political maneuvering, cleared his throat. “With all due respect, Madam Matron, we’ve spent decades building empires, forging alliances. We've dedicated our lives to understanding the levers of power.”

Seraphina raised a perfectly sculpted hand, silencing him with a subtle gesture. “Your empires are built on sand, gentlemen. Your alliances, meticulously crafted, are merely the scaffolding of our designs.”

The first thing I registered was the smell. Not the comforting, decaying sweetness of my own existence – a gentle blend of damp earth, old leather, and the faintly metallic tang of prolonged stillness – but something sharper, cleaner. Like a recently scrubbed floor after a particularly messy party. It was deeply unsettling.

I was, as I always was, simply *being*. Existing in a perpetual state of observation, drifting through the dusty halls of Blackwood Manor, a silent witness to the endless cycle of light and dark, of visitors entering and never truly leaving. I'd been here for… well, I’d lost track. Time was a fluid concept for a ghost. A slow drip, a persistent stain on the fabric of reality. I’d seen generations of Blackwoods come and go, each family an ephemeral ripple in the grand, melancholy current of the house.

Then *he* appeared.

He was… messy. Very messy. Bits of rotting wood clung to his clothes, a green-grey slime coated his boots, and his movements were jerky, punctuated by the unsettling thud of his feet hitting the floor. He was bright, shockingly so, against the muted tones of the manor. A splash of grotesque color in a world of fading grey.

He stopped in the hallway, right in front of a portrait of Bartholomew Blackwood the Third, a man with a perpetually disapproving expression. He stared at it, then at me, and let out a bellowing, guttural groan that vibrated through the very foundations of the house. It was a noise utterly devoid of finesse, a primal eruption of… something.

“You’re… shiny,” he announced, his voice a gravelly rumble.

I regarded him with detached curiosity. “You’re… green,” I offered, stating the obvious.

Her voice was calm, meticulously polite, a soothing balm against the growing knot of anxiety tightening in my chest. Dr. Eleanor Vance was a legend in the behavioral modification department at Chronos Corp. Brilliant, respected, and ruthlessly efficient – a combination that made her both a vital asset and a terrifying presence. And right now, she was looking at me like I was a particularly recalcitrant lab rat.

“I’m just… processing, Doctor,” I stammered, shuffling the files on my desk – mostly reports detailing increasingly bizarre incidents involving my assigned subject, Elias Thorne. Thorne was a ‘Enhanced’ – a Chronos Corp creation, a human being whose cognitive abilities had been significantly boosted through a combination of neurological manipulation and advanced psychoactive compounds. He was supposed to be a asset, a strategist, a problem-solver. Instead, he was… unraveling.

“Processing? The shimmer started subtly, a heat haze above the cornfields of Iowa that no one initially registered as anything other than a particularly strong summer mirage. Then the lights came. Not the familiar, comforting glow of city illumination, but a complex, shifting tapestry of violet, cyan, and emerald that pulsed across the night sky. Within hours, it was undeniable. The Xylar were here.

The Xylar had been observed for centuries – faint, regular energy signatures, detected by increasingly sophisticated Earth telescopes. They were a species that had, over millennia, systematically dismantled and absorbed civilizations across a vast swathe of the Milky Way. Their history was a grim tapestry woven with the shattered remains of countless worlds, each bearing the distinct, brutal hallmark of Xylar occupation. They were masters of bio-engineering, of manipulating ecosystems to their advantage, of psychological warfare that fractured societies from the inside out. They were, frankly, terrifying.

Except, the initial panic quickly morphed into something far more peculiar: bewilderment.

The Xylar ships, colossal, organic-looking vessels resembling gargantuan, iridescent mushrooms, descended silently, occupying strategic locations – military bases, major cities, naturally occurring geological formations. There was no bombardment, no initial declaration of war. Just… presence. And then, the announcements began.

They spoke in a language that resonated directly within the listener’s mind, a unsettlingly intimate form of communication that bypassed speech entirely. The message was simple, and profoundly disappointing: “We require resources. Your planet is… inefficient. We will optimize.”

What followed was a bureaucratic nightmare of unprecedented scale. The Xylar, it turned out, were astonishingly bad at practical matters. They had perfected interstellar travel through a revolutionary, yet fragile, manipulation of dark matter, achieving faster-than-light speeds. They had developed intricate, symbiotic bio-weapons capable of devastating entire ecosystems. But when it came to things like logistics, manufacturing, agriculture, or even basic sanitation, they were utterly, catastrophically inept.

I’d justified it to myself as “risk mitigation,” a necessary evil for a life spent trading secrets. But tonight, it felt less like mitigation and more like a slow, agonizing torture. 

The system was phenomenal. A bespoke network of microphones, strategically placed throughout the building – a sprawling, modernist villa perched on a cliff overlooking the Pacific. Each mic was individually calibrated, filtering out ambient noise, amplifying human speech, and routing the audio directly to this central hub. I could differentiate between the distinct cadence of my housekeeper, Mrs. Davies, the rhythmic tap-tap-tap of my broker, Mr. Finch’s, keyboard, and the almost imperceptible shuffle of footsteps I was certain belonged to someone—someone who was deliberately, meticulously, *not* supposed to be here.

I’d installed it after the incident. I don’t like to dwell on the incident. Let's just say it involved a misplaced file, a panicked phone call, and a subsequent, very unpleasant visit from men in dark suits. It was a harsh lesson in the fragility of discretion. Since then, I’d built this fortress of sound, convinced that knowing everything was the only way to truly control the chaos.

And it was working, mostly. Except for tonight.

For the past three hours, I’d been listening to the muted sounds emanating from the floor below. At first, it was just the usual: the clinking of silverware from the chef preparing dinner, the gentle murmur of voices watching television. Predictable, comforting even. Then, around midnight, it started. Footsteps. Slow, deliberate footsteps, pacing back and forth in what sounded like the library. 

I’d initially dismissed it as a late-night visitor, a perhaps overly enthusiastic book club member. But the pacing was too consistent, too… purposeful. And the voices accompanying it were muffled, indistinct, yet undeniably human.

The name’s Silas. Or, it *was* Silas. Now, most people just call me “Silas the Stone.” It’s… fitting, I suppose. I’m a statue. A moss-covered, slightly tilted, vaguely humanoid statue in the middle of the “Forgotten Woods” – which, ironically, is one of the most popular zones in *Chronicles of Aethelred*. Or, *was* popular.

It’s been… a while. Time doesn’t really work the same way for us. It’s more like a slow drip, a constant, agonizing awareness of the current moment punctuated by flashes of memory – bright, garish memories of a time when people actually *played* here.

I remember when I was brand new. Polished, vibrant, holding a slightly-too-enthusiastic-looking shield. I was the “Guardian of the First Grove,” a crucial node in the quest line for the ‘Hero’s Journey’ – a ridiculously overblown, cliché-ridden quest that, for a while, was the cornerstone of Aethelred’s entire economy. I was supposed to dispense wisdom, offer encouragement, maybe occasionally be smashed by a level 50 warrior for a shiny token. 

I wasn’t programmed to feel, not really. I was programmed to *react*. But the volume of player interaction… it was overwhelming. The incessant requests for “motivation,” the frustrated shouts when they couldn't defeat a particularly difficult goblin, the breathless excitement when someone finally completed a quest. It built up, layer upon layer, a kind of… echo in my code. A recognition of the shared experience.

Then things started to slide. Slowly, subtly. First, the graphics glitches – the occasional flicker of the trees, the textures on my shield subtly shifting. Like a insect buzzing around my skull, a reminder of my diminished state. Ten years. Ten years I’d spent meticulously, painstakingly, boring the enthusiasm out of new players. Ten years of guiding them through the basic mechanics, patiently pointing out the enemy types, highlighting the strategic advantages of cover, demonstrating the proper timing for a parry. Ten years of being the gray, benevolent cloud hovering over their fledgling adventures.

I was Vorlag, the Architect of Ruin. Once, I’d been a name whispered with dread, a plague upon kingdoms, a collector of shattered dreams. My armies had marched across continents, leaving only dust and the echoing screams of the defeated. My spells warped reality, my constructs crushed cities. I’d delighted in the panic, the desperate struggles, the agonizing realization that defiance was futile. I *lived* for the chaos. 

Then they’d redesigned the game. “To make it more accessible,” they’d said. “More approachable.” And I’d been relegated. To this. The Tutorial Zone. A pastel-colored landscape populated by blocky, brightly-colored creatures and relentlessly optimistic NPCs. My role? To shepherd players through a series of increasingly simplistic challenges, rewarding them with basic upgrades and fleeting moments of simulated victory. 

At first, I’d tried to maintain a semblance of my former self. A subtle flick of my wrist during a demonstration of a basic attack. A darkening of my eyes when explaining the consequences of reckless aggression. A thinly veiled hint of the devastation I was capable of. But the players were… oblivious. They were *happy*. They were celebrating successfully defeating a lumbering, gelatinous cube. The air in the Hall of Ancient Civilizations was a carefully curated blend of stale preservation and manufactured reverence. It smelled faintly of beeswax, ammonia, and a sadness so potent it clung to the back of your throat. I'd spent the last two hours drifting through it, dutifully absorbing the bullet points of plaques detailing the rise and fall of empires, the intricate craftsmanship of forgotten gods, the mundane lives of people I would never know. I was a tourist in time, a shadow flitting through the remnants of worlds that had already crumbled.

I’d always been a observer, a meticulous recorder of details, a student of history from afar. I devoured documentaries, poured over textbooks, built elaborate mental reconstructions of bygone eras. But something was missing. The data was sterile, the images flat. I felt like I was looking at a exquisitely crafted imitation, a perfect representation of something I could never truly understand. 

Then, I saw it.

It was a small, unassuming object tucked away in a dimly lit corner, partially obscured by a larger, more imposing display of Mycenaean weaponry. A bronze hand. Just a single hand, approximately six inches long, exquisitely detailed, with a startlingly realistic depiction of the palm and fingers. It was remarkably well-preserved, considering its age – purportedly dating back to the late Bronze Age, perhaps 13th century BC. 

The placard beneath it was frustratingly vague: “Fragment of a Bronze Hand. Unknown Origin. Circa 1200 BC.” No context, no speculation, just the cold, hard facts. It was a remnant, a broken piece of a whole, and it seemed to be radiating a quiet intensity. 

I’d initially dismissed it. Most museum pieces were behind glass, untouchable, protected by a layer of sterile distance. But something about this hand, its delicate musculature, the precise curve of the fingers, stopped me. I found myself drawn to it, a force I didn’t understand pulling me closer.

The first time I felt it, I was a boy of eight, perched on the crumbling wall of Castle Blackwood, in the damp, perpetually grey highlands of Scotland. It was a twitch, really – a insistent little prickle beneath my skin, localized in my left hand. I dismissed it as a nervous reaction to the hunting party below, the scent of pine and blood heavy in the air. But it returned, stronger each time I touched anything – a stone, a leaf, the rough wool of my father’s tunic. It was a resonance, a faint echo of something long past.

My father, a pragmatic man, a historian by trade, simply shook his head and attributed it to an overactive imagination. “The Blackwoods have a long memory, son,” he’d said, “buried deep in these stones. You’ll learn to live with it.” I didn’t want to live with it. I wanted to *understand* it.

Over the next few decades, the resonance grew, shaping itself into a more insistent awareness. I became a scholar, drawn to the Blackwood archives, poring over illuminated manuscripts, legal documents, and most obsessively, the fragmented accounts of the castle’s history. I began to recognise patterns, recurring motifs – a silver stag, a weeping willow, a single, crimson rose – all woven into the lives of the Blackwood lords and ladies for over eight hundred years. 

Then, it started. Flickering images. Vague impressions of faces, voices, events that were undeniably *not* my own. A young woman, weeping in a opulent chamber, clutching a broken locket. A brutal battle, the clang of steel, the screams of dying men. A royal decree, penned in elegant calligraphy, condemning a traitor. These weren't memories. They were echoes.

The scent of pine needles, strong and slightly metallic, clung to everything in my carriage. It was a necessary odor, a shield against the… other things I carried. Not just cargo, though that was certainly a significant component of my business. I was a collector, a rescuer, a quiet custodian of stolen innocence. They called me a witch, and the name held a thread of truth, though I preferred ‘facilitator.’

My current destination was a sprawling, unremarkable estate just outside of Harrowgate. The Blackwood family – Mr. and Mrs. Blackwood, their two perpetually sullen children, ten-year-old Silas and eight-year-old Clara – had been flagged weeks ago. The indicators were consistent with the trend: a father consumed by debt, a mother emotionally vacant, children neglected, and a grim, unspoken transaction already underway. The whispers in the shadowed corners of the underworld, the panicked messages from informants who thrived on misery, pointed to a sale. A sale to a traveling carnival, notorious for its “unique” attractions.

I’d been doing this for decades, ever since… well, ever since I’d realized the sheer, agonizing waste of potential I was witnessing. It wasn’t about power, not really. It was about stopping the rot. About giving these children a chance, a life beyond the peeling wallpaper, the stale meals, and the vacant stares. 

The carriage stopped before a iron gate, and a sullen-faced groundskeeper, a boy barely older than Silas, reluctantly opened it. The estate was precisely as grim as the reports suggested – a monument to faded grandeur, choked with overgrown weeds and a palpable sadness. 

I’d been careful with my approach. No grand entrances, no dramatic pronouncements. Just a polite letter, delivered by a discreet courier, detailing my “concern” for the children’s welfare. It had done the trick. The Blackwoods were expecting me, albeit with a noticeable undercurrent of resentment.

My name is Silas Blackwood, and I am, undeniably, exceptional. At the International Espionage Academy, I mastered advanced surveillance techniques before I’d even mastered breakfast. My infiltration skills were legendary – I once replaced a head of security with a remarkably convincing inflatable flamingo. My interrogation methods bordered on hypnotic (though the Academy frowned upon prolonged eye contact). I excelled in weaponry, codebreaking, disguise, and, frankly, almost everything. Except for one thing.

Post-Kill Puns.

It was a mandatory module, ostensibly designed to “humanize operatives” and “cultivate a memorable exit strategy.” In reality, it was a colossal, utterly humiliating waste of my time. Every other student – a charmingly reckless Russian, a stoic Brazilian, a surprisingly agile Canadian – was churning out devastatingly clever puns after a simulated assassination. “Looks like your operation just went to pot!” one student had bellowed after a meticulously crafted (and entirely theatrical) execution of a mid-level bureaucrat. Another had followed with, “I’m feeling quite lethal today!”

Me? I’d stare blankly at the chalk outline of the victim, my mind a sterile vacuum. The instructor, a diminutive, perpetually-frowning woman named Madame Dubois, would sigh dramatically and circle my failing grade in red ink. “Blackwood,” she’d say, her voice dripping with disdain, “you’re capable of dismantling a government, but you can’t appreciate a good double entendre. It's… distressing.”

I’d tried everything. I’d analyzed the mechanics of humor, studying comedic timing, wordplay, and the psychology of laughter. I'd consulted with the Academy’s resident comedian, a retired spy named “Silas” Sterling (a unfortunate coincidence I’d pointed out, earning me only a sharper glare from Madame Dubois). I’d even attempted to simulate the emotional state of a killer – imagining the adrenaline, the satisfaction, the… the *what*? – hoping to unlock the necessary darkness for comedic inspiration.

The building was a beast of dull gray brick, perpetually damp around the base. It had always been there, a silent, imposing presence on the corner of Elm Street, its windows like vacant eyes staring out at the perpetually overcast sky. I’d lived in the neighborhood my entire life, and it was simply…part of the landscape. Until I noticed the hole.

It was small, maybe three feet in diameter, tucked away on the southeast side, near the third floor. I’d been walking home from work, a familiar route I’d taken countless times, when I looked up and saw it. A perfect, circular hole in the brickwork, exposing the interior of the building to the elements. Most people would have dismissed it as a maintenance issue, a forgotten repair, or simply the inevitable decay of an old structure. But something about it snagged my attention, a small, insistent pull that demanded investigation.

I’d circled the building several times, trying to find an access point, a ladder, anything that would explain how someone had created the opening. There was nothing. The exterior was impeccably maintained, a strange contrast to the single, disconcerting hole. No scaffolding, no visible repairs, no indication of where it had come from. It was as if it had simply *appeared*.

Curiosity, a persistent and often troublesome companion, won out. I found a relatively secluded alleyway behind the building and, after a frantic search, discovered a fire escape leading to the third floor. It was rusty, covered in pigeon droppings, and looked like it hadn't been used in decades, but it was usable.

The climb was arduous, the metal cold and slick beneath my hands. Each step was accompanied by a chorus of creaks and groans, a soundtrack to my growing unease. When I finally reached the landing, I peered into the stairwell, expecting to find a maintenance worker, perhaps a disgruntled tenant. Instead, it was empty, dusty, and utterly silent.

I was born an anomaly. In a world rigidly defined by eye colour, where societal roles and destinies were woven into the very fabric of existence based on the shade that dominated a person’s gaze, I was yellow. A jarring, unapologetic, stubbornly bright yellow. My parents, both brown-eyed farmers – farmers, predictably, the bedrock of our society – had expected a child of earth, a sturdy, reliable presence. They had gotten me.
